blocks.content: The fundamental challenge facing TRAI stems from its recommendatory nature, leaving key policy decisions and spectrum management subject to executive discretion.

rows: Regulation of telecom/broadcasting tariffs, service standards, and policy advice
Adjudication of disputes and hearing appeals against TRAI decisions

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: TRAI was established under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997 to ensure fair and transparent regulatory environment for telecom services.
A primary structural challenge is that TRAI's recommendations regarding spectrum allocation and licensing terms are advisory and not binding on the Department of Telecommunications (DoT).
Regulatory overlap frequently occurs between TRAI, the Competition Commission of India (CCI), and MeitY over data protection and digital platforms.
Emerging technologies like 5G, Over-The-Top (OTT) communication services, and AI create regulatory lag and enforcement difficulties.
The 2000 amendment bifurcated powers by creating TDSAT to handle adjudicatory functions, restricting TRAI purely to regulatory and advisory roles.
TRAI is a statutory body established in 1997; it is NOT a constitutional or executive body.
TDSAT was set up via the 2000 TRAI Amendment Act to remove adjudicatory functions from TRAI's domain.
The Supreme Court affirmed that TRAI holds primary sectoral jurisdiction before issues can be escalated to competition regulators like CCI.
